power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: Bold marks the lowest overall rate; it does not differ significantly from VTC2 + WhisperX (p = .23).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .23", Sentence = "Bold marks the lowest overall rate; it does not differ significantly from VTC2 + WhisperX (p = .23)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 44 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. split_rttm_by_uri.py
--------------------
VTC1's apply.sh is run per recording FOLDER, producing one all.rttm per recording
whose rows are tagged with a per-clip URI (column 2). The downstream
whisperx_vtc_transcribe step, however, expects ONE timestamp file PER CLIP.

This script splits each recording's all.rttm by URI into per-clip all.rttm files:

    <dst>/<clip_uri>/all.rttm

Only clips that actually exist under the audio dir are emitted, which also drops
stale recordings left over in the shared VTC1 model output folder.

Usage:

text.text: Measuring how much of each language bilingual children hear and use in their daily lives requires transcribing long, naturalistic recordings, which is too costly to do by hand at scale.

We benchmarked four WhisperX-based automatic speech recognition pipelines, differing in how speech is located and attributed to speakers, against expert transcripts of 168 five-minute clips (14 hours) drawn from daylong home recordings of 14 Spanish-English bilingual preschoolers.
Word error rates across pipelines were high (69.5% to 82.0% overall), compared with 35.4% (key child) and 53.9% (adults) between expert coders.
Running a child-centered voice type classifier (VTC2) before transcription attributed words to speakers far better than labeling speakers afterwards; we retained this pipeline (WER = 71.4%).
Despite word-level errors, it preserved the rank order of clips; automated and manual counts of total and distinct words correlated at r = .83 to .93 for adults and the key child in each language.
Agreement rose further at the recording level.
Lexical diversity was recovered best: slopes for distinct words (0.79 to 0.88) were closer to one than for total words (0.53 to 0.77).
The proportion of Spanish was underestimated (adults: 77% vs. 89%; key child: 70% vs. 90%), largely because WhisperX output short English phrases on brief, unclear audio.

Open, inspectable pipelines can yield language-specific measures of bilingual adult input and child output, but precise word counts and language proportions require correction before direct interpretation.
These estimates, from one Spanish-English community, will need re-estimating in other populations.

Medir cuánto escuchan y usan los niños bilingües cada uno de sus idiomas en su vida cotidiana requiere transcribir grabaciones largas y naturalistas, lo cual resulta demasiado costoso para hacerlo manualmente a gran escala.

Evaluamos cuatro pipelines de reconocimiento automático del habla, todos basados en WhisperX y que se diferencían en cómo localizan el habla y cómo la atribuyen a los hablantes, en 168 fragmentos de cinco minutos (14 horas) extraídos de grabaciones domésticas de día completo de 14 niños preescolares bilingües español-inglés, usando transcripciones de expertos como referencia.
Las tasas de error de palabra fueron altas en todos los pipelines (69.5% a 82.0% en total), en comparación con 35.4% (niño focal) y 53.9% (adultos) entre transcriptores expertos.

Ejecutar un clasificador de tipo de voz centrado en el niño (VTC2) antes de la transcripción atribuyó las palabras al hablante correcto mucho mejor que clasificar a los hablantes después, y seleccionamos este pipeline.

A pesar de sus errores a nivel de palabra, preservó el orden relativo de los fragmentos en las medidas del entorno lingüístico: los conteos automáticos y manuales correlacionaron entre r = .83 y .93 para palabras totales y distintas, por separado para los adultos y el niño focal en cada idioma.
Agregar los conteos al nivel de la grabación aumentó aún más la concordancia.
La diversidad léxica fue la medida mejor recuperada: las pendientes para el número de palabras distintas oscilaron entre 0.79 y 0.88, más cercanas a uno que las de palabras totales (0.53 a 0.77).

La proporción de español fue subestimada (77% frente a 89% de las palabras de los adultos; 70% frente a 90% de las palabras del niño focal), en gran parte porque WhisperX produjo frases breves en inglés en segmentos de audio breves y poco claros.

Los pipelines abiertos e inspeccionables pueden producir medidas específicas por idioma del input de los adultos y de la producción del niño bilingüe, pero los conteos precisos de palabras y las proporciones por idioma requieren corrección antes de poder interpretarse directamente.
Estas estimaciones provienen de 14 grabaciones de una sola muestra comunitaria español-inglés y requerirán nueva estimación en otros contextos con poblaciones distintas.

Mesurer combien de chaque langue les enfants bilingues entendent et utilisent au quotidien exige de transcrire de longs enregistrements naturels, une tâche trop coûteuse manuellement à grande échelle.

Nous avons évalué quatre pipelines de reconnaissance automatique de la parole fondés sur WhisperX, différant dans la détection de la parole et son attribution aux locuteurs, par comparaison aux transcriptions expertes de 168 extraits de cinq minutes (14 heures) issus d'enregistrements à domicile sur une journée entière de 14 enfants bilingues espagnol-anglais d'âge préscolaire.
Les taux d'erreur sur les mots étaient élevés (69,5-82,0 % globalement), contre 35,4 % pour l'enfant cible et 53,9 % pour les adultes entre codeurs experts.

Appliquer un classifieur de type de voix centré sur l'enfant (VTC2) avant transcription attribuait bien mieux les mots aux locuteurs qu'un étiquetage ultérieur ; nous avons retenu ce pipeline (WER = 71,4 %).

Malgré les erreurs lexicales, il préservait le classement relatif des extraits ; les décomptes automatiques et manuels des mots totaux et distincts étaient corrélés (r = 0,83 à 0,93) pour les adultes et l'enfant cible dans chaque langue.
L'accord augmentait encore à l'échelle des enregistrements.
La diversité lexicale était la mieux restituée : les pentes pour les mots distincts (0,79-0,88) étaient plus proches de un que celles des mots totaux (0,53-0,77).

La proportion d'espagnol était sous-estimée (adultes : 77 % contre 89 % ; enfant cible : 70 % contre Children's everyday language environments are linked to later language and literacy outcomes (Anderson et al., 2021; Weiss et al., 2022).
text.formatted: La proportion d'espagnol était sous-estimée (adultes : 77 % contre 89 % ; enfant cible : 70 % contre Children's everyday language environments are linked to later language and literacy outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anderson et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Weiss et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Making sense of language environments is far from trivial: children must track who is speaking, distinguish talk directed at them from overheard talk, and separate both from electronic media, siblings, and the overlapping sounds of ordinary home life.

For the many children growing up with more than one language, there is another level of complexity to contend with, because which language they hear often shifts with speaker, setting, and activity (Fishman, 1965; Orena et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For the many children growing up with more than one language, there is another level of complexity to contend with, because which language they hear often shifts with speaker, setting, and activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Fishman, 1965;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Orena et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Spanish-English bilingual children in the United States, of whom there are more than six million under age nine (Migration Policy Institute, n.d.), are one large and well-studied case of this broader pattern.
For these children, their linguistic environment is not a single stream of input in one language, but a shifting array of opportunities to hear and use both languages.
These opportunities are rarely evenly distributed.
English dominates schooling and the wider society, putting heritage languages like Spanish at risk of attrition once formal schooling begins (Duursma et al., 2007).
text.formatted: English dominates schooling and the wider society, putting heritage languages like Spanish at risk of attrition once formal schooling begins <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Duursma et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding how bilingual children extract signal from noise during the transition to schooling requires methods that can recover key features of the home language environment from complex, naturalistic data.
Recent years have seen rapid advances in the hardware and software needed to gain a more complete picture of young children's language environments.

Small, wearable recorders can capture long stretches of a child's day, and many labs now use either the LENA (Language ENvironment Analysis) system (Gilkerson & Richards, 2008) or consumer-grade alternatives to collect naturalistic daylong audio recordings (Cristia et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Small, wearable recorders can capture long stretches of a child's day, and many labs now use either the LENA (Language ENvironment Analysis) system <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Gilkerson & Richards, 2008)</ref> or consumer-grade alternatives to collect naturalistic daylong audio recordings <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cristia et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: LENA software and other automated tools make it possible to measure the quantity of children's language input and output across the day, such as how many adult words a child hears, how many vocalizations the child produces, and how many conversational turns take place.

These tools capture only how much speech occurs, not its content: they do not identify what is said or which language is being spoken, and no currently available system estimates how much of each language a child hears and uses.
Such measures would address basic questions about bilingual acquisition and applied questions about supporting heritage language maintenance.

Manual transcription can answer these questions, but the cost is high (Kremin et al., 2022; Orena et al., 2020). Sun et al. (2024) estimate that expert transcription requires roughly five hours for every ten minutes of preschool classroom audio.
text.formatted: Manual transcription can answer these questions, but the cost is high <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kremin et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Orena et al., 2020)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sun et al. (2024)</ref> estimate that expert transcription requires roughly five hours for every ten minutes of preschool classroom audio.

text.text: Bilingual home recordings add further demands: transcribers must understand both languages, mark language switches, and distinguish speech from multiple adults and children (Wu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Bilingual home recordings add further demands: transcribers must understand both languages, mark language switches, and distinguish speech from multiple adults and children <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Wu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These requirements make fully manual transcription and analysis difficult to scale, even for moderate-sized corpora.
To bypass the time required for full transcription, alternative approaches manually code language use directly from audio files without transcribing the speech verbatim (Marchman et al., 2017).
text.formatted: To bypass the time required for full transcription, alternative approaches manually code language use directly from audio files without transcribing the speech verbatim <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Marchman et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Sampling-based coding reduces this further, but the effort still scales with the size of the corpus (Cychosz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Sampling-based coding reduces this further, but the effort still scales with the size of the corpus <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cychosz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Automatic transcription could provide another way around this bottleneck.
Critically, the measures researchers and clinicians often seek from naturalistic data, such as the amount and lexical diversity of talk in each language, are aggregate quantities.

Errors that would be unacceptable in a verbatim transcript may still leave such aggregates recoverable, which makes the relevant question not whether automatic transcription is accurate, but whether it is accurate enough for the uses to which it is put.

Automatic transcription has become an increasingly accessible option in recent years, especially with the release of Whisper (Radford et al., 2023), which is freely available and trained on about 680,000 hours of multilingual audio.
text.formatted: Automatic transcription has become an increasingly accessible option in recent years, especially with the release of Whisper <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref>, which is freely available and trained on about 680,000 hours of multilingual audio.

text.text: Whisper itself is a speech recognition model: it converts audio into words, but its built-in handling of silence and non-speech is limited, and it can produce text where no one is speaking.

WhisperX (Bain et al., 2023) wraps Whisper with additional models: a voice activity detector from pyannote.audio (Bredin et al., 2020), which finds the stretches of audio that contain speech before Whisper transcribes them (and can optionally label who speaks when), and an alignment model that assigns each word a precise timestamp.
text.formatted: WhisperX <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bain et al., 2023)</ref> wraps Whisper with additional models: a voice activity detector from pyannote.audio <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bredin et al., 2020)</ref>, which finds the stretches of audio that contain speech before Whisper transcribes them (and can optionally label who speaks when), and an alignment model that assigns each word a precise timestamp.

text.text: Recent studies have begun to test whether Whisper and Whisper-based pipelines such as WhisperX can support developmental and clinical research on child language environments.

Reported word error rates (WER), the proportion of words inserted, deleted, or substituted relative to a human transcript, range from roughly 15% in structured classroom recordings to over 50% in unconstrained daylong audio (Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025; Raviv et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Reported word error rates (WER), the proportion of words inserted, deleted, or substituted relative to a human transcript, range from roughly 15% in structured classroom recordings to over 50% in unconstrained daylong audio <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Raviv et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sun et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Tang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To date, most studies using Whisper have focused on adult speech in controlled environments, and much less work has applied Whisper to daylong recordings, child speech, and bilingual environments.
Bilingual child speech is the least studied of these, and presents difficulties on two fronts.
The first is child speech itself, which is underrepresented in Whisper's training data and differs from adult speech in articulation, fundamental frequency, and disfluency.
Off-the-shelf Whisper captured about half of the words spoken by typically developing children and fewer than one in six words spoken by children with Down syndrome (McGonigle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Off-the-shelf Whisper captured about half of the words spoken by typically developing children and fewer than one in six words spoken by children with Down syndrome <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(McGonigle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The second is the bilingual setting.

ASR systems perform worse on language varieties that are underrepresented in training data (Koenecke et al., 2020), and heritage speaker Spanish with English insertions may be similarly disadvantaged.
text.formatted: ASR systems perform worse on language varieties that are underrepresented in training data <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Koenecke et al., 2020)</ref>, and heritage speaker Spanish with English insertions may be similarly disadvantaged.

text.text: Compounding this, Whisper sometimes translates speech instead of transcribing it.

Part of its training data paired speech in one language with text in another, including about 125,000 hours of speech translated into English (Radford et al., 2023), so the model learned to associate audio with its meaning in another language as well as with the words spoken.
text.formatted: Part of its training data paired speech in one language with text in another, including about 125,000 hours of speech translated into English <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref>, so the model learned to associate audio with its meaning in another language as well as with the words spoken.

text.text: Because Whisper also settles on a single language for each stretch of audio it processes (up to 30 seconds), rather than for each utterance, a switch within that stretch may come out as a translation, yielding text that appears monolingual and gives no indication that a switch occurred.

The closest benchmark comes from Wu et al. (2025), who tested several Whisper-based approaches on recorded Mandarin-English parent-child sessions and reached word error rates of 35% for child speech and 30% for speech containing both languages.
text.formatted: The closest benchmark comes from <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Wu et al. (2025)</ref>, who tested several Whisper-based approaches on recorded Mandarin-English parent-child sessions and reached word error rates of 35% for child speech and 30% for speech containing both languages.

text.text: We are not aware of comparable work on Spanish-English speech, though Albudoor and Peña (2022) used a commercial speech recognition system to score bilingual children's responses on a standardized language assessment, identifying Developmental Language Disorder (DLD) about as accurately as human scoring.
text.formatted: We are not aware of comparable work on Spanish-English speech, though <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Albudoor and Peña (2022)</ref> used a commercial speech recognition system to score bilingual children's responses on a standardized language assessment, identifying Developmental Language Disorder (DLD) about as accurately as human scoring.

text.text: These studies show that ASR can support bilingual child language research, but they leave open the setting that motivates the present study: naturalistic, daylong Spanish-English parent-child recordings collected in the home.
The present study had two aims.
First, we developed an ASR pipeline for naturalistic daylong recordings of Spanish-English bilingual home environments and benchmarked its performance against human-transcribed clips.

Second, we tested whether the pipeline's output preserves aggregate measures of language input and child output that researchers and clinicians rely on, such as the quantity of talk and the number of different words used in each language.

Social-interactionist theories of language development propose that children are naturally driven to communicate with caregivers in their environment and thus build language skills through meaningful, reciprocal interactions (Bruner, 1981; Vygotsky, 1978).
text.formatted: Social-interactionist theories of language development propose that children are naturally driven to communicate with caregivers in their environment and thus build language skills through meaningful, reciprocal interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bruner, 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Vygotsky, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Research has shown that the quantity and features of the input children hear in their daily lives are reflected in measures of child language skills, particularly vocabulary knowledge (Coffey & Snedeker, 2025).
text.formatted: Research has shown that the quantity and features of the input children hear in their daily lives are reflected in measures of child language skills, particularly vocabulary knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Coffey & Snedeker, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, passive exposure to input does not tell the full story.
Children construct their language through active use when they initiate interactions and respond to caregiver prompts (Tomasello, 2003).
text.formatted: Children construct their language through active use when they initiate interactions and respond to caregiver prompts <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Tomasello, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Active language use is thought to provide an opportunity to process new forms more fully (Swain, 2005) as well as elicit feedback from caregivers (Warlaumont et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Active language use is thought to provide an opportunity to process new forms more fully <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Swain, 2005)</ref> as well as elicit feedback from caregivers <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Warlaumont et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: While input and use are considered key factors in the language acquisition of all children, their distinct roles are more separable in bilingual children.

Because bilingual children's input is distributed across two languages, studies have shown that greater relative exposure in a language is associated with stronger skills in that language (Pearson et al., 1997; Thordardottir, 2011), as well as language-specific associations between the absolute quantity of input and skills (Marchman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Because bilingual children's input is distributed across two languages, studies have shown that greater relative exposure in a language is associated with stronger skills in that language <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Pearson et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Thordardottir, 2011)</ref>, as well as language-specific associations between the absolute quantity of input and skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Marchman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Because bilinguals may hear more of a language than they actively use, it is possible to explore the unique role of language use separate from language input in bilingual children.

For example, Ribot et al. (2018) found that Spanish-English bilingual children's (parent-reported) code-switches to English predicted their growth in English expressive vocabulary beyond their reported English input.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Ribot et al. (2018)</ref> found that Spanish-English bilingual children's (parent-reported) code-switches to English predicted their growth in English expressive vocabulary beyond their reported English input.

text.text: In addition to varying among bilingual children, input and use in each language also vary within individuals over time, especially during the transition to schooling.

Because schooling tends to prioritize learning in the societal language, school entry often represents a significant change in the everyday language experiences of children who primarily use a heritage language at home.

Unsurprisingly, studies have shown that during the first years of school, children's societal language input and use tends to increase, and their heritage language input and use tends to decrease (Hammer et al., 2011; Wong Fillmore, 1991).
text.formatted: Unsurprisingly, studies have shown that during the first years of school, children's societal language input and use tends to increase, and their heritage language input and use tends to decrease <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hammer et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Wong Fillmore, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: This large variability among and within individuals makes it possible to examine the role of input and use in bilingual language acquisition.
However, most studies to date have relied on parent reports of input and use.

A few have examined the amount of input bilingual children hear in each language using daylong recordings (Cychosz et al., 2025; Kan et al., 2020; Orena et al., 2020) and at least one study used longitudinal structured observations of bilingual parent-child dyads to examine change over time in parent input and child use across languages (Luo et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A few have examined the amount of input bilingual children hear in each language using daylong recordings <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cychosz et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kan et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Orena et al., 2020)</ref> and at least one study used longitudinal structured observations of bilingual parent-child dyads to examine change over time in parent input and child use across languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Luo et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Being able to efficiently estimate the quantity of input and output in each language in daylong recordings would make these measures usable at scale in basic research on bilingualism and child language acquisition, adding to this literature.
Beyond the amount of input, as children approach school age, the quality of input becomes increasingly important (e.g., Rowe & Snow, 2020).
text.formatted: Beyond the amount of input, as children approach school age, the quality of input becomes increasingly important (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Rowe & Snow, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One widely used measure of input quality is lexical diversity, or the number of different words in adult speech heard by the child.

In a recent meta-analysis, Anderson et al. (2021) found that input quality (as indexed by lexical diversity or syntactic complexity) was a stronger predictor of child language outcomes than input quantity, and the association increased with child age.
text.formatted: In a recent meta-analysis, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Anderson et al. (2021)</ref> found that input quality (as indexed by lexical diversity or syntactic complexity) was a stronger predictor of child language outcomes than input quantity, and the association increased with child age.

text.text: Though this meta-analysis only included studies with English language outcomes, similar results have been obtained for bilinguals' heritage language outcomes (e.g., Daskalaki et al., 2020; Gámez et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Though this meta-analysis only included studies with English language outcomes, similar results have been obtained for bilinguals' heritage language outcomes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Daskalaki et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Gámez et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, input quality is rarely captured in daylong recordings due to the expense and time required to transcribe the data.
In addition to its utility as a measure of input quality, lexical diversity can also be used as a proxy for the child's lexical knowledge.

Previous work has drawn on the number of different word types to index the expressive vocabulary knowledge of the child for descriptive research (Adamson et al., 2021), child outcome measures in intervention studies (e.g., Harden et al., 2026) and clinical identification of language disorders (Kapantzoglou et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Previous work has drawn on the number of different word types to index the expressive vocabulary knowledge of the child for descriptive research <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adamson et al., 2021)</ref>, child outcome measures in intervention studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Harden et al., 2026)</ref> and clinical identification of language disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kapantzoglou et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Despite their theoretical importance and clinical applications, few studies have examined the quantity and quality of input and use in bilingual development using daylong recordings of home environments.

Because longer recordings can mitigate observer effects and capture more ecologically valid data across more contexts, being able to do so has the potential to reveal a more precise, holistic picture of individual differences and their relation to later outcomes.
Researchers have used daylong recordings to capture children's everyday language exposure and use for many decades.

Early efforts recorded full days of school-age children's speech to estimate how much children talk (Wagner, 1985), and later work recorded nearly all of one child's home experience from birth to age three (Roy et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Early efforts recorded full days of school-age children's speech to estimate how much children talk <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Wagner, 1985)</ref>, and later work recorded nearly all of one child's home experience from birth to age three <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Roy et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: With the development of the proprietary LENA system in the late 2000s (Gilkerson & Richards, 2008), daylong recordings became more widely accessible, and studies using this approach have proliferated since then (Ganek et al., 2018; Greenwood et al., 2018).
text.formatted: With the development of the proprietary LENA system in the late 2000s <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Gilkerson & Richards, 2008)</ref>, daylong recordings became more widely accessible, and studies using this approach have proliferated since then <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ganek et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Greenwood et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: LENA pairs a wearable recorder with a closed analysis pipeline that returns adult word count (AWC), child vocalization count (CVC), and conversational turn count (CTC) over five-minute, hour-long, or full-day recording windows.
These automated measures make daylong recordings usable at scale, and have yielded insights into the role of input and use in child language development.
For example, all three measures have been linked to later vocabulary and literacy outcomes (Gilkerson et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For example, all three measures have been linked to later vocabulary and literacy outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gilkerson et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Wang et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: CVC has also been used to explore how children's language production increases with age and varies by child internal and environmental factors (Bergelson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: CVC has also been used to explore how children's language production increases with age and varies by child internal and environmental factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bergelson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Although validity studies often report low correlations between LENA's CTC and transcriber counts of conversational turns, CTC is nevertheless associated with positive outcomes such as socioemotional competencies (Gómez & Strasser, 2021) and increased activation in brain areas used for language (Romeo et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Although validity studies often report low correlations between LENA's CTC and transcriber counts of conversational turns, CTC is nevertheless associated with positive outcomes such as socioemotional competencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gómez & Strasser, 2021)</ref> and increased activation in brain areas used for language <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Romeo et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although the LENA system was trained on recordings from primarily English-speaking, monolingual U.S. households, it performs adequately to well in non-English language contexts.
Across 14 validation studies of non-English contexts, correlations ranged from .67 to .93 for AWC and .71 to .80 for CVC (Cristia et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Across 14 validation studies of non-English contexts, correlations ranged from .67 to .93 for AWC and .71 to .80 for CVC <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cristia et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that LENA is able to rank order recordings by the amount of input and output in non-English languages.
However, three key limitations have impeded the usefulness of the LENA system for work in bilingual contexts.

First, large absolute differences between LENA measures and human-transcriber counts have raised concerns about systematic undercounting of adult and child speech in other languages (Marchman et al., 2020; Meera et al., 2025).
text.formatted: First, large absolute differences between LENA measures and human-transcriber counts have raised concerns about systematic undercounting of adult and child speech in other languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Marchman et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Meera et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the LENA system returns overall word counts, but cannot identify the languages being spoken.

For bilingual development research, this is a serious constraint, because the amount of input a child receives and the amount of talk they produce in each language are often the variables of interest.
The third limitation compounds the first two.

Because the LENA system is closed-source, researchers cannot inspect where errors occur, retrain components for new populations, or publish a fully reproducible processing workflow (Baker et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Because the LENA system is closed-source, researchers cannot inspect where errors occur, retrain components for new populations, or publish a fully reproducible processing workflow <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baker et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In response to these constraints, researchers have developed open-source alternatives for processing daylong recordings collected with LENA recorders or other wearables.

These algorithms are typically trained on daylong recordings from a more diverse set of languages and geographical settings, and can be used to identify speech segments and label speaker types (Lavechin et al., 2020), and then estimate the quantity of adult speech in phonemes, syllables, and words (Automatic LInguistic unit Count Estimator, or ALICE; Räsänen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: These algorithms are typically trained on daylong recordings from a more diverse set of languages and geographical settings, and can be used to identify speech segments and label speaker types <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lavechin et al., 2020)</ref>, and then estimate the quantity of adult speech in phonemes, syllables, and words (Automatic LInguistic unit Count Estimator, or ALICE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Räsänen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: But ALICE, like LENA, produces counts rather than transcripts, and it does not assign words to languages.
Pipelines that include automatic speech recognition promise to provide a different kind of output: not only how much speech occurred, but what was said and in which language(s).
Currently, parent report is the dominant approach to quantifying bilingual children's input and output in each language.

Several standardized protocols have been developed, including diary-based reports (Place & Hoff, 2011), and cumulative and hourly estimates (e.g., Byers-Heinlein et al., 2020; DeAnda et al., 2016; de Cat et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Several standardized protocols have been developed, including diary-based reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Place & Hoff, 2011)</ref>, and cumulative and hourly estimates (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Byers-Heinlein et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">DeAnda et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">de Cat et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These instruments have many useful applications, but parent-reports are not as strong a predictor of child language outcomes as direct observations (Marchman et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These instruments have many useful applications, but parent-reports are not as strong a predictor of child language outcomes as direct observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Marchman et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, as children enter school and spend more time outside the home and with conversation partners other than the primary caregiver, the child's current and historical input and output becomes more challenging and burdensome for caregivers to report.

Parent-reported measures typically produce a single measure of relative exposure in each language, rather than capture moment-to-moment variation or distinguish between child input and output across speakers and settings.

Manual transcription of all caregiver and child talk is more time consuming than collecting parent-reports, but has been used with shorter, structured observations (e.g., Luo et al., 2020; Quiroz et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Manual transcription of all caregiver and child talk is more time consuming than collecting parent-reports, but has been used with shorter, structured observations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Luo et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Quiroz et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Full transcripts allow for more precise word counts and more detailed coding schemes of parent and child language behaviors, but are rarely feasible with longer recordings or large corpora.

Several studies using daylong recordings have listened to a subset of the data and annotated the language(s) used in the sampled segments without transcription (e.g., Marchman et al., 2017; Orena et al., 2020; Wood et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Several studies using daylong recordings have listened to a subset of the data and annotated the language(s) used in the sampled segments without transcription (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Marchman et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Orena et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Wood et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Although less time-intensive than transcription, precision varies by sampling strategy, rater reliabilities, and the amount of talk in each coded segment. Cychosz et al. (2021) addressed the question of how many segments need to be coded in a given recording by developing a Python-based protocol that randomly samples 30-second segments for coding until a stable estimate is reached.
text.formatted: Although less time-intensive than transcription, precision varies by sampling strategy, rater reliabilities, and the amount of talk in each coded segment. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Cychosz et al. (2021)</ref> addressed the question of how many segments need to be coded in a given recording by developing a Python-based protocol that randomly samples 30-second segments for coding until a stable estimate is reached.

text.text: This approach works well if bilingual research assistants are available and the metric of interest is relative exposure and use.
Across these approaches, no current method yields full-day estimates of both input and child output in each language at the lexical level.
Automated transcription offers a route to measures that sampling-based coding cannot produce.
While automated transcription holds promise for quantifying child output in each language, children's speech remains a poor fit for many off-the-shelf ASR systems.

Most systems are trained primarily on adult speech, because child corpora tend to be small, restricted for privacy reasons, and rarely included in the web-scraped audio used to train models like Whisper.
Because of this discrepancy in training data, accuracy drops when these models are applied to children (McGonigle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Because of this discrepancy in training data, accuracy drops when these models are applied to children <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(McGonigle et al., 2024</ref>).

text.text: Children's voices have higher fundamental and formant frequencies than adults', and their speech varies more from one production to the next (Lee et al., 1999); young children also produce frequent non-word vocalizations, such as babbling and unintelligible speech, which ASR tends to drop or turn into words (McGonigle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Children's voices have higher fundamental and formant frequencies than adults', and their speech varies more from one production to the next <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lee et al., 1999)</ref>; young children also produce frequent non-word vocalizations, such as babbling and unintelligible speech, which ASR tends to drop or turn into words <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(McGonigle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These properties affect both acoustic and language modeling, so errors in child speech are not simply a matter of background noise or recording quality.

Whisper is frequently used in recent developmental work because it is freely available and its large-scale weakly supervised training reportedly makes it robust across speakers, accents, and recording conditions (Radford et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Whisper is frequently used in recent developmental work because it is freely available and its large-scale weakly supervised training reportedly makes it robust across speakers, accents, and recording conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Even so, child speech remains difficult, and reported error rates vary widely with the children's age and the and filler words (Tang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Even so, child speech remains difficult, and reported error rates vary widely with the children's age and the and filler words <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Tang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These errors matter in developmental data, because brief child productions are often analytically important.
If these frequent short utterances are missed, then child word counts will be biased downward.

Daylong child-centered audio adds another layer of difficulty. Kocharov and Räsänen (2025) evaluated Whisper on four English-language daylong corpora and reported a mean WER of 51% when all annotated speech was scored.
text.formatted: Daylong child-centered audio adds another layer of difficulty. <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kocharov and Räsänen (2025)</ref> evaluated Whisper on four English-language daylong corpora and reported a mean WER of 51% when all annotated speech was scored.

text.text: Yet their study also shows why WER is not the only relevant outcome.
After filtering to utterances that ASR could reasonably be expected to transcribe, mean WER fell to 18%.

More important for measurement, word log-frequencies estimated from automatic transcripts were strongly correlated with estimates from manual annotation: r = 0.92 overall and r = 0.98 for words occurring at least five times in the automatic transcript.
This finding matters for the present work because it separates two questions that are often collapsed.
A transcript can be imperfect at the word level and still preserve some aggregate linguistic measures.
We ask whether that possibility extends to Spanish-English home recordings, where the measures must also be separated by speaker and by language.
One study has addressed this measurement question directly using monolingual classroom recordings (Sun et al., 2024).
text.formatted: One study has addressed this measurement question directly using monolingual classroom recordings <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Sun et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Their pipeline combines the voice type classifier (VTC; Lavechin et al., 2020), an open-source model that detects speech in child-centered recordings and labels each stretch by speaker type (key child, other child, female adult, male adult), with Whisper transcription, and aligns the output to expert coding in ELAN.
text.formatted: Their pipeline combines the voice type classifier (VTC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lavechin et al., 2020)</ref>, an open-source model that detects speech in child-centered recordings and labels each stretch by speaker type (key child, other child, female adult, male adult), with Whisper transcription, and aligns the output to expert coding in ELAN.

text.text: On preschool classroom audio from child-worn recorders and teacher-worn recorders, they report WERs of 14.7% for teachers and 15.0% for children.
Their most useful contribution for the present study is not the low WER itself but their decision to evaluate derived measures.

Whisper-derived and expert-derived estimates were strongly related for measures such as mean length of utterance, question rate, response latency, and lexical alignment; MLU correlations were r = .87 for teachers and r = .80 for children.
This measurement-validity approach is the one we adopt here.
Transcription accuracy is only part of the problem.
Word counts are only meaningful when they are attributed to the right speaker, so the system that segments the audio by speaker matters as much as the transcription model.

Only one study we are aware of has evaluated Whisper-based pipelines on bilingual child speech. Wu et al. (2025) drew on 53 telehealth sessions, about 20 hours of Mandarin-English parent-child interaction, collected during the Mandarin-English Receptive Language Screener task.
text.formatted: Only one study we are aware of has evaluated Whisper-based pipelines on bilingual child speech. <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Wu et al. (2025)</ref> drew on 53 telehealth sessions, about 20 hours of Mandarin-English parent-child interaction, collected during the Mandarin-English Receptive Language Screener task.

text.text: Their comparison of six cascaded pipelines found that pairing a speaker segmentation system with Whisper performed best, reaching WERs of .35 on child speech and .30 on code-switched speech.
Our study follows a similar pipeline-comparison logic, but the setting differs: Spanish-English daylong home recordings rather than structured telehealth assessment sessions.
The studies reviewed above point to a different question than whether ASR "works" on child speech and daylong recordings.

For bilingual developmental research, the more useful question is whether an automated pipeline can recover the measures that researchers and clinicians rely on, separately for each speaker and each language, from the kind of naturalistic recordings they collect in the field.
Three limitations in prior work motivate the present benchmarking study.

First, the strongest evaluations of Whisper on naturalistic parent-child speech have been conducted almost entirely on monolingual English data (Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025; McGonigle et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2025), leaving open whether those findings transfer to speech where the system must also resolve which language is being spoken.
text.formatted: First, the strongest evaluations of Whisper on naturalistic parent-child speech have been conducted almost entirely on monolingual English data <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">McGonigle et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Tang et al., 2025)</ref>, leaving open whether those findings transfer to speech where the system must also resolve which language is being spoken.

text.text: Second, the bilingual benchmarks that exist concentrate on Mandarin-English interaction (Hai et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), and the one Spanish-English study used structured test items rather than spontaneous home interaction (Albudoor & Peña, 2022).
text.formatted: Second, the bilingual benchmarks that exist concentrate on Mandarin-English interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hai et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Wu et al., 2025)</ref>, and the one Spanish-English study used structured test items rather than spontaneous home interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Albudoor & Peña, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Third, where ASR-derived measures have been validated against expert coding (Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025; Sun et al., 2024), that validation has not extended to measures separated by language.
text.formatted: Third, where ASR-derived measures have been validated against expert coding <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sun et al., 2024)</ref>, that validation has not extended to measures separated by language.

text.text: For bilingual households, where the amount and quality of input and child talk in each language are often the variables of interest, this is the measure most in need of testing.
Existing work establishes that automatic transcription of children's speech is error-prone, and that some aggregate measures survive those errors.
Whether that holds for bilingual home recordings, where measures must be separated by speaker and by language, has not yet been tested.
The current study addresses two research questions: 1.
Which automatic speech recognition pipeline configuration produces the most accurate transcription of daylong bilingual home recordings, and how does accuracy vary by speaker and language?
To what extent do language environment measures computed from automatic transcripts agree with those from manual transcripts?
We first benchmark four WhisperX-based ASR pipelines on 14 daylong Spanish-English bilingual parent-child recordings collected in participants' homes.
From each recording, we randomly sampled twelve 5-minute clips spread across the morning, midday, afternoon, and evening, to obtain 60 minutes of audio from each recording.
The resulting benchmark contains 168 clips, or approximately 14 hours of audio, with expert reference transcription.
The pipelines differ in which speaker classifier they use and whether it runs before or after transcription.
We compare them using word error rate (WER).
We then ask whether the best-performing pipeline preserves aggregate measures that researchers would normally compute from expert transcripts.

For each 5-minute clip, we compare automated and expert-coded counts of total, English, and Spanish words separately for adults and the key child, along with two measures of lexical diversity: number of different words and type-token ratio.
We repeat these comparisons with each child's twelve clips summed into a single recording-level total; these results are reported in the supplementary material.
We also compare the proportion of words spoken in each language.

Relative and absolute measures can be derived from one another but represent distinct constructs, and while most work on bilingual environments relies on relative exposure, absolute input may be the better predictor of language outcomes (De Houwer, 2014; Marchman et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Relative and absolute measures can be derived from one another but represent distinct constructs, and while most work on bilingual environments relies on relative exposure, absolute input may be the better predictor of language outcomes (De Houwer, 2014; <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Marchman et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This measurement validity analysis follows the logic of Sun et al. (2024) and Kocharov and Räsänen (2025): an automated transcript does not have to be perfect at the word level to be useful, but it must preserve the quantities that researchers plan to interpret.
text.formatted: This measurement validity analysis follows the logic of <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sun et al. (2024)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kocharov and Räsänen (2025)</ref>: an automated transcript does not have to be perfect at the word level to be useful, but it must preserve the quantities that researchers plan to interpret.

text.text: To summarize, this study contributes a benchmark of naturalistic, daylong recordings with preschool-aged Spanish-English bilingual children and their families.

It tests whether automatically identifying who is speaking before transcription improves accuracy, and whether the resulting transcripts preserve how much each speaker said in each language and how varied their vocabulary was.

More broadly, the goal is to evaluate whether open, inspectable pipelines can provide the kind of per-language measurement that closed, count-only systems such as LENA cannot offer for bilingual households.

The audio came from a larger randomized controlled trial supporting Spanish and English development at home and at school, which collected 137 daylong LENA recordings in the greater Houston, TX area, where a large share of households use Spanish at home (Lacarte et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The audio came from a larger randomized controlled trial supporting Spanish and English development at home and at school, which collected 137 daylong LENA recordings in the greater Houston, TX area, where a large share of households use Spanish at home <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Lacarte et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Families were eligible for that trial if the primary caregiver used Spanish with the child at least half the time and the child scored below the 16th percentile on an English vocabulary screener at preschool entry.
Each recording follows one child through an ordinary non-school day.
All recordings used here were completed at baseline, before randomization.
Forty-five families had not consented to human listening of their audio and were excluded, leaving 92 recordings available.
From these we selected 14 recordings.

One was chosen deliberately, early on, because it contained close to equal amounts of English and Spanish, which made it useful for developing the transcription protocol and training coders on code-switched speech.

The other 13 were drawn systematically so that the sample would mirror the 92 available recordings rather than over-represent any one kind of child: we matched the gender split of the available pool (39.1% male, 60.9% female), for 5 boys and 8 girls (6 boys in all, with the deliberately chosen recording), and within each gender we spread the selection across the age range instead of taking consecutive children.
The resulting 14 children averaged 4.93 years of age (SD = 0.40), close to the 4.83-year average of the pool they came from, and 10 of the 14 had caregivers who reported using only Spanish with them.
Table 1 provides the individual characteristics.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> provides the individual characteristics.

text.text: Transcribing 14 full days by hand was not feasible, so from each recording we randomly sampled twelve 5-minute clips from across the day, to obtain 60 minutes of audio per child.
We spread the sampled clips across the morning, midday, afternoon, and evening to represent the full day.
We excluded partial clips shorter than 300 seconds and any clip inside a window a parent had asked us not to listen to.
This gave 168 clips and roughly 14 hours of audio.
We used 5-minute clips because that length is conventional in daylong-recording research and is short enough to transcribe by hand at this volume (McGonigle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We used 5-minute clips because that length is conventional in daylong-recording research and is short enough to transcribe by hand at this volume <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(McGonigle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Four Spanish-English bilingual coders transcribed all 168 clips in ELAN (Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics, The Language Archive, 2026), following the ACLEW annotation scheme (Soderstrom et al., 2021) and CHAT conventions (MacWhinney, 2000).
text.formatted: Four Spanish-English bilingual coders transcribed all 168 clips in ELAN (Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics, The Language Archive, 2026), following the ACLEW annotation scheme <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Soderstrom et al., 2021)</ref> and CHAT conventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(MacWhinney, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: All four completed the ACLEW (Analyzing Child Language Experiences around the World) Gold Standard training (Casillas et al., 2017), scoring above .90 agreement on utterance segmentation and utterance annotations on both the English and Spanish versions of that test, and were then trained further on this project's conventions.
text.formatted: All four completed the ACLEW (Analyzing Child Language Experiences around the World) Gold Standard training <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Casillas et al., 2017)</ref>, scoring above .90 agreement on utterance segmentation and utterance annotations on both the English and Spanish versions of that test, and were then trained further on this project's conventions.

text.text: Manual annotation involved three tasks: segmenting the audio by speaker (who speaks when), identifying the language of each segment (which language is being spoken), and transcribing the speech (what is being said).
Regarding speakers, coders marked where each utterance started and ended and who produced it.
Speaker tiers were named following ACLEW conventions, which distinguish individual speakers (e.g., FA1, FA2 for separate female adults).
Coders assigned speakers to an adult category on the basis of voice quality and conversational role rather than any known age, so adult here means a speaker the coders judged to be past adolescence.

For comparison with the pipelines, these labels were collapsed to match the four categories produced by the voice type classifiers (Section 2.2): key child (KCHI), other child (OCH), male adult (MAL), and female adult (FEM).
All non-target children were combined into OCH, and multiple adults of the same gender were combined into a single category.

Regarding language, coders marked language at the word level, enclosing embedded English in curly braces (e.g., tú juega {like this}), so that a single utterance can contribute words to both languages.

Proper nouns, language-neutral interjections, and English-origin words in ordinary use in U.S. Spanish were treated as belonging to the surrounding language (e.g., oh, okay, dámelo was considered Spanish only).

Regarding transcription, coders transcribed all speech addressed to or overheard by the target child except speech from younger siblings, which was set aside so that coder effort went to the two things the study is about: what the child says and what caregivers say to them.
Because speech from other children was therefore transcribed only when those children were roughly the target child's age or older, the other-child category is incomplete and we do not evaluate it.
Coders also did not transcribe speech from televisions, tablets, or other electronic sources.
WhisperX's speech detector and Whisper itself do not distinguish such speech from live talk.

The voice type classifiers were trained on annotations that exclude electronic speech and so should ignore much of it, but not reliably; electronic speech they mistakenly include remains in the automated output and is one known source of words the pipelines produce that the coders did not.
Every clip was reviewed by a second transcriber and then checked by a script enforcing the project's conventions.
The final reference contains 37,131 words, 88.9% of them Spanish.
Table 2 breaks this down by speaker and language; per-recording totals are in the supplementary material (Table A1).
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> breaks this down by speaker and language; per-recording totals are in the supplementary material (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A1</ref>).

text.text: Given the difficulty of the task and the noise in daylong home recordings, a word error rate of 0% is not a realistic expectation, even for human transcribers.

We therefore measured how closely two trained humans agree on the same clips, so that agreement between the pipelines and the coders could be compared with agreement between coders, a realistic ceiling for automated transcription.
Eight clips were transcribed independently by more than one coder, two during training and six later in the process.
Four were transcribed by all four coders and four by two transcribers each, resulting in 24 independently completed transcripts.
We compared coders to each other in exactly the way we later compared the pipelines to the coders, using the same text cleanup and the same word matching (Sections 2.4.1 and 2.3.1).
This yields a word error rate between two humans.
Because neither coder is considered the gold standard reference, we divided the errors by the average length of the two transcripts rather than by one of them.
We assessed agreement between coders on all three annotation tasks (Section 2.1.2).
For transcription, we used the word error rate described above.

Computed separately by speaker and by language, word error rate also reflects disagreements about who was speaking and which language was spoken, because a word credited to a different speaker or language counts as an error, but it mixes these disagreements with disagreements about the words themselves.

To measure agreement on segmenting the audio by speaker and identifying the language directly, we used Krippendorff's α, computed on whether a stretch of audio contained speech, who was speaking, whether the speech was intelligible, and which language it was in.

This is an agreement score that runs from 0 (agreement no better than chance) to 1 (perfect agreement), and unlike more familiar alternatives like Cohen's κ, it can handle clips coded by different numbers of coders.
Intervals come from 2,000 bootstrap resamples over clips; per-clip values are in Table A2.
text.formatted: Intervals come from 2,000 bootstrap resamples over clips; per-clip values are in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">A2</ref>.

text.text: To assess inter-coder agreement for the quantity of words transcribed, we additionally computed intraclass correlations using a one-way random effects model.
Deriving per-speaker word counts from daylong recordings requires two steps.
The first is speaker segmentation: finding the stretches that contain speech and labeling each one with who spoke.
The second is transcription: converting each stretch of audio into written words.
Figure 1 shows this process.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> shows this process.

text.text: We held transcription model constant so that differences between pipelines could be attributed to speaker segmentation.

All four used WhisperX (Bain et al., 2023), which combines two independently developed models: a voice activity detector (VAD) from pyannote.audio (Bredin et al., 2020), which finds speech in whatever audio it is given, and Whisper large-v3 (Radford et al., 2023), which transcribes it and detects its language automatically.
text.formatted: All four used WhisperX <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bain et al., 2023)</ref>, which combines two independently developed models: a voice activity detector (VAD) from pyannote.audio <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bredin et al., 2020)</ref>, which finds speech in whatever audio it is given, and Whisper large-v3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref>, which transcribes it and detects its language automatically.

text.text: Whenever we write WhisperX below, both models are involved, including when WhisperX is given segments cut by a speaker classifier.
Any stretch that WhisperX transcribed in a language other than English or Spanish, even after a second detection attempt, was discarded.
We selected WhisperX because it is freely available, open source, and the system most commonly used in recent benchmarking work with child speech.

The four pipelines cross two decisions at the segmentation step: which voice type classifier labels the speakers (VTC1, Lavechin et al., 2020 , or VTC2, Charlot et al., 2026), and whether it runs before transcription, cutting the audio into the stretches WhisperX transcribes, or after, labeling stretches that WhisperX found for itself.
text.formatted: The four pipelines cross two decisions at the segmentation step: which voice type classifier labels the speakers (VTC1, <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lavechin et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">, or VTC2, Charlot et al., 2026)</ref>, and whether it runs before transcription, cutting the audio into the stretches WhisperX transcribes, or after, labeling stretches that WhisperX found for itself.

text.text: These choices also affect language identification: because WhisperX detects language over the audio window it receives, the way a pipeline cuts the audio determines what the language detector sees.

The first two pipelines follow the arrangement used in previous studies: let the speech recognition system find and transcribe the speech itself, as Tang et al. (2025) did, and work out who was speaking afterwards with a speaker classifier, as Sun et al. (2024) did.
text.formatted: The first two pipelines follow the arrangement used in previous studies: let the speech recognition system find and transcribe the speech itself, as Tang et al. (2025) did, and work out who was speaking afterwards with a speaker classifier, as <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sun et al. (2024)</ref> did.

text.text: We included this arrangement for comparison with that earlier work, and call these the post-hoc pipelines, because speakers are labeled after transcription.
In these pipelines, speech is found by the voice activity detector (VAD) that WhisperX runs before transcription.
Whisper on its own detects speech poorly and often produces text for silence or noise, which is why WhisperX adds a separate detector.
We refer to this detector as WhisperX-VAD.

WhisperX merges the speech it detects into chunks of up to 30 seconds, Whisper transcribes each chunk, and each resulting stretch is then labeled by checking which speaker region it overlaps in a separate run of a voice type classifier.

Because WhisperX receives the whole 5-minute clip in these pipelines, it chooses a language once, from the first 30 seconds of the clip; any segment that Whisper's language detector then identified as Spanish was transcribed again with Spanish specified.
We ran this once with VTC1 and once with VTC2.
The two post-hoc pipelines share one transcript and differ only in their speaker labels, so comparing them shows the effect of the classifier alone.

Each also has a counterpart below that uses the same classifier but runs it before transcription (WhisperX-VAD + VTC1 versus VTC1 + WhisperX, and WhisperX-VAD + VTC2 versus VTC2 + WhisperX), so comparing each pair shows the effect of running the classifier before or after transcription.

One reason to let WhisperX set the boundaries is that Whisper was trained on 30-second windows of audio, and WhisperX hands it chunks of similar length, whereas a classifier run first hands it shorter pieces.

The drawback is that the pyannote.audio detector was trained mainly on adult speech, with spontaneous child-centered conversation rare in its training data, whereas the voice type classifiers were trained on daylong child-centered recordings like ours.
In addition, speaker labels copied from one tool's stretches of speech onto another's are only as good as how well the two sets of stretches line up.
Two details of this labeling affect the results.

When a stretch overlapped more than one speaker region we assigned it by the fixed priority KCHI > OCH > FEM > MAL, which favors catching key-child speech; because a whole stretch takes one label, a stretch containing two speakers is credited entirely to the higher-priority one.
text.formatted: When a stretch overlapped more than one speaker region we assigned it by the fixed priority KCHI > OCH > FEM > MAL, which favors catching key-child speech; because a whole stretch takes one label, a stretch containing two speakers is credited entirely to the higher-priority one.

text.text: Stretches overlapping no speaker region, or only VTC1's catch-all label for speech from an unidentified speaker, could not be credited to anyone and were dropped from all scoring, including the overall score.
The third pipeline replaces that first step with the voice type classifier of Lavechin et al. (2020), VTC1, which does the segmentation and speaker labeling in one pass before transcription.
text.formatted: The third pipeline replaces that first step with the voice type classifier of <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lavechin et al. (2020)</ref>, VTC1, which does the segmentation and speaker labeling in one pass before transcription.

text.text: Each VTC1 segment is then passed to WhisperX, whose pyannote.audio VAD runs within the segment before Whisper transcribes it; speech that this detector rejects inside a segment is not transcribed.
VTC1 is built on the same pyannote.audio architecture as that detector, but it was trained on daylong child-centered recordings rather than mainly on adult speech.

Speaker classifiers built for child-centered audio have been paired with Whisper before, in preschool classroom recordings, where speakers were labeled after transcription (Sun et al., 2024), and in head-mounted camera recordings of infants and toddlers (Long et al., 2024), but neither study tested whether the classifier should run before or after transcription.
text.formatted: Speaker classifiers built for child-centered audio have been paired with Whisper before, in preschool classroom recordings, where speakers were labeled after transcription <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Sun et al., 2024)</ref>, and in head-mounted camera recordings of infants and toddlers <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Long et al., 2024)</ref>, but neither study tested whether the classifier should run before or after transcription.

text.text: Our four pipelines compare the two orders directly.
The fourth pipeline uses VTC2 (Charlot et al., 2026), the successor to VTC1, trained on a larger and more varied collection of child-centered daylong recordings, to do the same job.
text.formatted: The fourth pipeline uses VTC2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Charlot et al., 2026)</ref>, the successor to VTC1, trained on a larger and more varied collection of child-centered daylong recordings, to do the same job.

text.text: We expected it to perform best of the four, but it had not previously been evaluated on bilingual audio of this kind.
Knowing which pipeline performs best does not tell us how much of the remaining error comes from each step, so we ran two further conditions to separate them.
In Human-TS + WhisperX (TS for timestamps), WhisperX is handed the coders' own utterance boundaries and speaker labels, so speaker segmentation is done by humans.

As in the other pipelines, WhisperX's speech detector still runs within each segment it receives, so it can discard parts of a coder-marked utterance it does not judge to be speech; the remaining error is therefore mainly, though not exclusively, transcription error.
This is a reference point rather than a ceiling: because it inherits human boundaries, it is not guaranteed to beat every automated front end on every measure.
In VTC2-NoLang + WhisperX, everything matches VTC2 + WhisperX except that stretches WhisperX transcribed in a language other than English or Spanish are kept instead of discarded.
The difference between the two shows what is gained by discarding output in languages the household does not use.
Because the text cleanup removes characters outside the Latin alphabet (Section 2.4.1), output in languages such as Chinese, Japanese, or Korean is not scored in either condition.

WhisperX reports the language it used for each stretch of audio it transcribes, but what that stretch is differs across pipelines: in the pipelines where a speaker classifier or the coders segment the audio first, it is a single segment, whereas in the post-hoc pipelines it is a whole 5-minute clip.

To label language the same way across all pipelines, we instead ran an off-the-shelf language-identification program, langdetect, on the text of each automated utterance and counted all of its words under the resulting label.
For the selected pipeline, VTC2 + WhisperX, this choice makes little difference: the langdetect label matched the language WhisperX reported for 99.5% of words (Section 3.4).
This is a simplification with a known cost: an utterance that switches language partway through is counted entirely as one language, whereas the coders labeled language word by word.
That mismatch puts a ceiling on how closely the automated language proportions can match the manual ones, and we return to it in the Discussion.
We measured transcription accuracy with word error rate (WER), computed with jiwer (Vaessen, 2025).
text.formatted: We measured transcription accuracy with word error rate (WER), computed with jiwer <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Vaessen, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: WER aligns the automatic transcript with the human one and counts the edits needed to turn one into the other: where I is the number of insertions (i.e., the number of words the pipeline added); D is the number of deletions (i.e., the number it missed); S is the number of substitutions (i.e., the number it got wrong); and N is the number of reference words in the human transcript.
WER can exceed 100%, because the automatic transcript can be longer than the manual one.
We computed WER three ways, each answering a different question.
For overall WER we joined everything said in a clip, in time order and regardless of speaker, and compared the two transcripts.
This measures overall transcription disagreement regardless of who spoke.

For WER by speaker we joined all utterances belonging to one speaker type, either the key child or the adults (MAL and FEM together), and compared those; this reflects how well the pipeline identifies the speaker as well as how well it transcribes, so a word transcribed correctly but credited to the wrong speaker counts as an error.
For WER by language we did the same thing for all words labeled English and all words labeled Spanish.
For this comparison, words take the language of the coders' utterance label rather than the word-level markup, so English words inside a Spanish utterance count as Spanish.

We used utterance labels here because the automated transcripts are labeled one utterance at a time (Section 2.2.5); splitting the reference word by word while the automated output is split by utterance would create errors from the mismatch alone.
The word counts and language proportions (Section 2.3.2) use the coders' word-level markup.
Words in utterances that the coders marked as mixed (1,040) or did not mark as English or Spanish (2,130), 8.6% of the reference, count toward overall WER but not toward either language.
Two things follow from how the language comparison is built.

Since a word enters the English or Spanish comparison according to the language it was labeled with, this measure reflects language labeling as much as transcription: an utterance transcribed correctly but labeled with the wrong language counts as insertions on one side and deletions on the other.
And where a clip's human transcript contains no words of a given language, there is nothing to compare against, so automated words in that language go uncounted.
This affects 4.6% of the selected pipeline's words (1,189 of 25,915).
Nearly all of them are English words in the 53 clips in which the coders labeled no utterance as English; no Spanish words are affected, since every scored clip contained Spanish.
The rest come from some of the 11 clips, described below, that were excluded from scoring because they contained no transcribable key-child or adult speech.
