Other-child speech is excluded from the speaker and word-count analyses, since the coders did not transcribe all of it, but is retained in the overall and by-language comparisons, which do not depend on who is speaking.
Eleven of the 168 clips contain no transcribable words from the key child or the adults.

In seven the coders marked nothing at all; in the other four the only annotations were non-speech vocalizations such as laughs and noises, or speech marked unintelligible, all of which the text cleanup removes (Section 2.4.1).
With nothing on the human side to compare against, an error rate cannot be defined, so all error rates are computed on the remaining 157 clips.
These are the language environment measures used to answer the second research question.
For every clip we counted, from both the human and the automated transcripts, how many words each speaker type produced in each language.
We also counted the number of different words each speaker used in a clip, after the cleanup described in Section 2.4.1 so that spelling and inflectional variants do not count as separate words.
For comparability with Tang et al. (2025) we also computed the type-token ratio, the number of different words divided by the total.
text.formatted: For comparability with <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Tang et al. (2025)</ref> we also computed the type-token ratio, the number of different words divided by the total.

text.text: Because type-token ratio is known to depend on sample length, we treat the number of different words as the primary measure of lexical diversity.
Finally, we computed the proportion of each speaker's words that were Spanish.
This measure requires the pipeline to recognize the words, assign them to the right speaker, and label their language correctly.

Coverage differs across these measures, because a clip can only contribute where the relevant speech exists: word counts are available for all 168 clips, number of different words for the 158 clips with adult speech and the 161 with key-child speech in either the manual or the automated transcript, and WER for the 157 scored clips.
Choosing a pipeline.
We compared the four pipelines on overall WER and on WER for the key child and for the adults, across the 157 scored clips.
Errors were summed within each recording and the 14 resulting rates were averaged, so that every family counts equally no matter how much talk its recording contains.
All resampling was likewise done over recordings rather than clips, because clips from the same recording share speakers, acoustics, and language habits and so are not independent.

Differences between pipelines were tested with a paired bootstrap (Koehn, 2004): we drew 10,000 random resamples of the 14 recordings and asked how often a difference as large as the observed one arose by chance (two-tailed).
text.formatted: Differences between pipelines were tested with a paired bootstrap <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Koehn, 2004)</ref>: we drew 10,000 random resamples of the 14 recordings and asked how often a difference as large as the observed one arose by chance (two-tailed).

text.text: Confidence intervals came from a separate set of 5,000 resamples.
Full intervals and pairwise tests are in the supplementary material.
Because one recording had been chosen deliberately rather than sampled, we repeated the comparison without it.
We had initially planned to choose the pipeline for the measurement analysis on overall WER alone.

We deviated from this plan because the two pipelines with the lowest overall WER did not differ significantly (Section 3.2), and instead chose between them on WER by speaker, the quantity every language environment measure depends on.

To explain differences between the classifiers, we also compared each classifier's adult segments with the coders' adult utterances: the total time labeled adult, where that time fell relative to the coders' annotation, and how often a coder utterance overlapped more than one classifier segment.
For the chosen pipeline we compared automated and human estimates clip by clip, separately for each speaker type and language, using Pearson correlations and the slopes of straight-line fits.
The two answer different questions: the correlation says whether the pipeline ranks clips in the right order, the slope says whether it recovers the right amount.

Clips where the coders recorded no words in the language concerned are shown in the figures but left out of the fits, since they offer no quantity for a slope to be measured against and would drag the slope toward one.
Proportions of Spanish words were compared clip by clip in the same way.
All audio was converted to 16 kHz mono 16-bit WAV with ffmpeg, the format both
Human and automated transcripts were cleaned identically before being compared, so that differences in formatting could not register as errors.

Cleanup removed CHAT markup, stripped punctuation and accents, lower-cased everything, removed characters outside the Latin alphabet, merged hyphenated compounds, and applied the standard Spanish contractions (de el to del, a el to al).

Words the coders had marked unintelligible were removed from the human transcript, so that a pipeline is not penalized for speech the coders themselves could not make out; words it produced in those places still count as insertions.

text.text: The word error rate between two human coders was 35.4% for key-child speech, 53.9% for adult speech, and 46.0% overall.
For other-child speech, which could be compared on only two clips (650 words), it was 68.2%.
For key-child speech, the 35.4 percentage points consisted of 19.7 points of substitutions, 7.9 of deletions, and 7.8 of insertions.
For adult speech, the 53.9 points consisted of 21.3 points of substitutions, 19.7 of deletions, and 12.9 of insertions.
Agreement on whether speech was present was α = .63, 95% CI [.44, .76].
Agreement on who was speaking was α = .47, 95% CI [.26, .64]; this value covers the key child and the two adult categories and does not include the key-child versus other-child decision.
When the female and male adult categories were combined, speaker agreement was α = .48, 95% CI [.28, .61].

These values are lower than agreement on whole utterances would be, because α was computed over 100-ms slices of audio: two coders who mark the same utterance but place its start or end a few hundred milliseconds apart disagree on every slice in between.

Agreement on whether speech was present ranged from .63 to .86 in seven of the eight clips; one clip, which also showed the only substantial confusion between key child and adults, was .13 and lowers the pooled value.
Agreement on whether a stretch of speech was intelligible was α = .48, 95% CI [.37, .54].
Agreement on the language of an utterance was α = .49, 95% CI [.24, .64].
Among utterances that both coders assigned to English or Spanish, language agreement was α = .88, 95% CI [.66, .97], and α = .94 when computed word by word.
Agreement on the number of words transcribed per clip was assessed with a one-way random-effects intraclass correlation (single measure, absolute agreement).
The ICC was .94, 95% CI [.81, .99], for adult words and .97, 95% CI [.92, .99], for key-child words.
Our first research question asked which pipeline configuration produces the most accurate transcription and how accuracy varies by speaker and language.

Of VTC1's adult-labeled time, 50% fell within the coders' adult utterances, 21% on speech the coders attributed to children, and 29% on stretches with no coded speech; for VTC2 the shares were 76%, 4%, and 20%.
VTC1 did not split adult utterances more often than VTC2 (12% vs. 14% of utterances overlapped two or more adult segments), and its adult segments were longer (median 1.32 vs.

Most of them (91%) fell where the coders had transcribed no speech, compared with 6% of the words VTC2 did assign to a speaker, and they came mostly in multi-word Spanish stretches rather than short stock phrases.

This pattern is consistent with electronic speech from televisions or tablets, which the coders did not transcribe and VTC2 was trained to ignore (Section 2.1.2), although the coders did not mark media, so we cannot confirm it directly.

text.text: In summary, VTC2 + WhisperX had the lowest WER for both the key child and adults, and was the only pipeline that did not perform markedly worse on one of the two.
The other pipelines failed in different ways for the two speaker types.

The post-hoc pipelines performed worst on key-child speech: because each WhisperX chunk takes a single label and the key child has priority, adult words were credited to the key child, inflating the key child's transcript with insertions and leaving the adults' transcript with deletions.
VTC1 + WhisperX performed worst on adult speech, because VTC1 labeled more audio as adult speech than the coders did, much of it on children's speech or on stretches without coded speech.
On overall WER, which ignores who is speaking, three of the four pipelines differed by less than four points; the differences between pipelines lie mainly in crediting words to the right speaker.
Pipeline selection.

Because the two pipelines with the lowest overall WER did not differ significantly, we selected between them on WER by speaker rather than on overall WER as initially planned (Section 2.3.3), and carried VTC2 + WhisperX forward to the measurement analysis (Section 3.5).
As a sensitivity check, we repeated the comparison excluding the recording that was selected rather than randomly sampled.
The ranking of the pipelines was unchanged on overall WER and on WER for either speaker type.
When WhisperX was given the coders' own utterance boundaries and speaker labels (Human-TS + WhisperX), overall WER was 71.5%, compared with 71.4% for VTC2 + WhisperX.
The same held by speaker:
Human-TS + WhisperX did not differ significantly from VTC2 + WhisperX on key-child speech (76.0% vs.
75.3%) and was only slightly lower on adult speech (70.4% vs.

Replacing VTC2's segments with the coders' own therefore did little to reduce error, which indicates that the remaining error in VTC2 + WhisperX comes mainly from transcription rather than from finding and labeling speech.
Even with human boundaries, WER remained well above the disagreement between two human coders (35.4% for key-child speech, 53.9% for adult speech, and 46.0% overall; Section 3.1).
Differences from this control for every pipeline and speaker type are given in Table A9.

text.text: By speaker.
Averaged across recordings, WER was 75.3% for the key child, 78.1% for male adults (13 recordings; one contained no male-adult speech), 74.6% for female adults, and 72.1% for adults combined.

78.1% averaged over recordings).
Deletions were the largest error type in every speaker category: 4,930 of the key child's 9,473 errors and 2,677 of male adults' 4,628.
Expressed as a rate, deletions accounted for 36.8 of the key child's 75.3 WER points.
Insertions ranged from 231 to 663 across speaker categories.
Pooled across the corpus, Spanish accounted for 20,451 errors against 30,023 reference words (12,128 deletions, 7,469 substitutions, 854 insertions), a WER of 68.1%.
English accounted for 5,032 errors against 3,622 reference words (2,885 insertions, 1,617 substitutions, 530 deletions), a WER of 138.9%.
Insertions into English amounted to 79.7% of English reference words.
WER can exceed 100% because insertions enter the numerator but not the denominator.
Language labeling.
The utterance-level language labels agreed with the language in which WhisperX transcribed for 99.5% of words (25,774 of 25,915).
Under the coding conventions (Section 2.1.2), language-neutral interjections within Spanish talk (e.g., hm, okay, no, yeah) were coded as Spanish; the pipeline labeled them English.
Such interjections made up 982 of the 7,159 words in utterances the pipeline labeled English (14%), or 769 (11%) excluding no, which is also an ordinary Spanish word.
Of the 2,888 utterances the pipeline assigned to English, 1,251 (43%) consisted of one of the 25 most frequent short utterances (listed in Table A10).

text.text: Three of them (thank you, yeah, and you) accounted for 588 utterances.
Across the whole reference corpus, the coders transcribed thank you three times; the pipeline produced it 241 times (Table 4).

text.text: Two other short English words, no and okay, were produced by the pipeline less often than the coders transcribed them (97 vs. 311 and 78 vs.
We aligned each stock-phrase segment with the coders' annotation for the same moment.
For 44% of them, the coders recorded no transcribable speech: either nothing at that point in the clip (18%) or only a laugh, a noise, or unintelligible speech (27%).
Across all English output, 1,830 words (26% of the words the pipeline labeled English) were produced at moments with no transcribable speech in the reference.
For example, across two seconds of one clip in which the coders marked three vocalizations and no words, the pipeline produced you, you, and thank you.

Where a stock phrase overlapped speech the coders transcribed, the coders had labeled the utterance it overlapped most as Spanish 55% of the time and as English 13% of the time; most of the rest was speech the coders did not label as either language.
Empty segments.
In 2,847 segments, the speaker classifier marked a region as speech but the pipeline kept no words.

In 2,824 of them (99%), WhisperX had transcribed the stretch in a language other than English or Spanish, most often Chinese, Korean, or Japanese (8,559 words in all), and the pipeline discarded that output (Section 2.2).
At most the remaining 23 could reflect WhisperX's speech detector finding no speech within the segment.
The 2,847 empty segments total 77 minutes, or 9% of the benchmark audio.
Of these, 493 overlapped another talker.
By speaker, 1,432 belonged to the key child, 606 to female adults, 553 to other children, and 256 to male adults.

text.text: In an informal reading of the transcripts (not a scored analysis), we saw WhisperX translate speech into English rather than transcribe it only in the post-hoc pipelines, never in VTC2 + WhisperX, consistent with these pipelines choosing one language per 5-minute clip (Section 2.2.1).

Rendering Spanish speech, babbling, laughter, or play sounds as words in other languages did occur in VTC2 + WhisperX; most of that output was in languages other than English or Spanish and was discarded, leaving the empty segments described above.
Our second research question asked to what extent language environment measures computed from automatic transcripts agree with those from manual transcripts.

We compared clip-level measures from VTC2 + WhisperX with those from the manual transcripts (Table 5): word counts, two measures of lexical diversity (number of different words and type-token ratio), and the proportion of words in each language, each computed separately for adults and the key child.
text.formatted: We compared clip-level measures from VTC2 + WhisperX with those from the manual transcripts (Table <ref type="table">5</ref>): word counts, two measures of lexical diversity (number of different words and type-token ratio), and the proportion of words in each language, each computed separately for adults and the key child.

text.text: Word counts.
Automated and manual word counts were correlated for every speaker and language, r = .86 to .93 (Table 5, Figure 3).
text.formatted: Automated and manual word counts were correlated for every speaker and language, r = .86 to .93 (Table <ref type="table">5</ref>, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3</ref>).

text.text: The slopes of the regression of automated on manual counts were all below one, ranging from 0.53 (key-child Spanish) to 0.77 (key-child English): for every additional word the coders transcribed, the pipeline returned between about half and three quarters of a word, so the automated counts increasingly fell short as the amount of talk rose.

In 68 of the 93 adult clips and 74 of the 89 key-child clips in which the coders recorded no English, the pipeline returned a non-zero English count; for Spanish, this happened in 5 of 19 adult clips and in none of 14 key-child clips.

Summed over each recording, VTC2 + WhisperX word counts correlated with manual counts at r = .97 for English and r = .96 for Spanish, compared with r = .93 and .94 for Human-TS + WhisperX; these were the highest correlations of any pipeline, and the 95% confidence intervals overlapped across pipelines (Figure A1).
text.formatted: Summed over each recording, VTC2 + WhisperX word counts correlated with manual counts at r = .97 for English and r = .96 for Spanish, compared with r = .93 and .94 for Human-TS + WhisperX; these were the highest correlations of any pipeline, and the 95% confidence intervals overlapped across pipelines (Figure <ref type="figure">A1</ref>).

text.text: The number of different words correlated at r = .83 to .89, with slopes from 0.79 to 0.88 (Table 5, Figure 4).
text.formatted: The number of different words correlated at r = .83 to .89, with slopes from 0.79 to 0.88 (Table <ref type="table">5</ref>, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">4</ref>).

text.text: For each speaker and language, the slope for number of different words was higher than the corresponding word-count slope.
Type-token ratios correlated at r = .27 to .62, with slopes from 0.18 to 0.62.
In Spanish, automated type-token ratios were higher than manual ones: .78 vs. .62 for the key child and .76 vs. .63 for adults.
In English they were close: .77 vs. .77 for the key child and .81 vs. .83 for adults.
Proportion of words in each language.

Spanish accounted for 89.3% of adult words and 90.4% of key-child words in the coders' transcripts, compared with 77.2% and 70.3% in the VTC2 + WhisperX transcripts, a difference of about 12 percentage points for adults and 20 for the key child.

The clip-level proportion of Spanish words correlated with the manual values at r = .59 for adults (n = 147) and r = .50 for the key child (n = 151), well below the correlations for word counts and for the number of different words.

Our main finding is that in naturalistic Spanish-English daylong audio recordings, a Whisper-based pipeline can recover aggregate language measures that characterize input and output in each language.
Count-based measures were more reliable than proportions, and type-based measures came closest to the manual values.
Importantly, these count-and type-based measures preserve the rank-ordering of clips but are biased in the absolute magnitude of counts.

Bilingualism and child language researchers have long argued for the importance of capturing absolute measures of input rather than relying on relative exposure to describe bilingual environments (De Houwer, 2014).
text.formatted: Bilingualism and child language researchers have long argued for the importance of capturing absolute measures of input rather than relying on relative exposure to describe bilingual environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(De Houwer, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This approach takes us closer to that goal, though the remaining bias means the counts are not yet interpretable as exact quantities.
It also allows us to capture absolute measures of child output, which are of theoretical importance in research on heritage language maintenance (Ribot et al., 2018; Unsworth et al., 2018).
text.formatted: It also allows us to capture absolute measures of child output, which are of theoretical importance in research on heritage language maintenance <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Ribot et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Unsworth et al., 2018</ref>).

text.text: Below we discuss the results behind this finding: how the pipeline should be arranged, what its high word error rate means, and whether its word counts can stand in for manual ones.

We then discuss how the pipeline performs on absolute and relative measures of bilingual input and output, why it underestimates Spanish, and what it offers beyond currently available automated algorithms for processing daylong recordings.
We selected VTC2 + WhisperX, in which VTC2 identifies the speaker before Whisper transcribes: its overall WER did not differ significantly from the lowest (WhisperX-VAD + VTC2; 71.4% vs.
69.5%), and it credited far more words to the right speaker (Section 3.2).
Which speaker classifier a pipeline uses, and when it runs, mattered less for transcription than for crediting words to the right speaker.
On overall error, three of the four pipelines finished within four points of one another and within two points of the condition using the coders' own utterance boundaries (Section 3.2).
Because the coders' own boundaries did not lower overall error, the remaining error in the best pipelines comes mainly from transcription rather than from finding and labeling speech.
The exception was the pipeline using VTC1 as the first step, which performed worst overall and especially on adult speech.

Its errors on adult speech were dominated by insertions and substitutions rather than deletions, and the segment analysis shows that VTC1 labeled too much audio as adult speech, rather than cutting adult turns into short pieces: VTC1 marked far more audio as adult speech than the coders did, and half of it fell on children's speech or on stretches the coders did not transcribe (Section 3.2).
This pattern is consistent with earlier evaluations showing that VTC1 favors recall over precision, detecting most adult speech but also labeling non-adult audio as adult (Lavechin et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with earlier evaluations showing that VTC1 favors recall over precision, detecting most adult speech but also labeling non-adult audio as adult <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lavechin et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Whisper therefore transcribed that audio as adult talk, adding words to the adult transcript.
VTC2, run in the same position, did not have this problem.
A classifier's benefit therefore depends on the specific classifier and on the recordings it is applied to, and has to be measured rather than assumed.
Larger differences among pipelines emerged once words had to be credited to a speaker.

When speakers are labeled after transcription, each chunk Whisper transcribes, up to 30 seconds long, takes a single label, and the key child is given priority, so a chunk that contains both the child and an adult is credited entirely to the child.

This explains why, in the post-hoc arrangement, adult words went largely missing from the adult transcript while the child's transcript filled with insertions: the words had been transcribed but were credited to the wrong speaker.

This is a property of the arrangement, not of the classifier: it happened with VTC1 and VTC2 alike, and switching to the better classifier left error on key-child and adult speech essentially unchanged.
Running the classifier first avoids the problem, because every stretch Whisper transcribes already belongs to one speaker.
Letting VTC2 decide what Whisper transcribes did not make the words more accurate, but it credited far more of them to the right speaker.

Whisper translating speech into English, which we saw only in the post-hoc pipelines (Section 3.4; Table A11),is consistent with how these pipelines choose a language: once per 5-minute clip rather than once per segment (Section 2.2.1).
text.formatted: Whisper translating speech into English, which we saw only in the post-hoc pipelines (Section 3.4; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A11</ref>),is consistent with how these pipelines choose a language: once per 5-minute clip rather than once per segment (Section 2.2.1).

text.text: Researchers who need measures for particular speakers should therefore run the speaker classifier before transcription.
Labeling afterwards is adequate only when the total transcript, and not speaker assignment, is all that matters.

Determining who is speaking is thus a central problem in child-centered recordings rather than a minor step after transcription, as studies of noisy classroom audio have also found (Sartaz Khan et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Determining who is speaking is thus a central problem in child-centered recordings rather than a minor step after transcription, as studies of noisy classroom audio have also found <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Sartaz Khan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sun et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The WERs of the best pipeline are high, but they cannot be interpreted without considering how far apart two trained coders are on the same audio.
Expert coders differed substantially on all speech types, suggesting that much of this audio is hard to transcribe reliably, even for trained listeners.
Our best pipeline was about twice as far from the reference as a second coder on key-child speech (75.3% against 35.4%), but only about a third further on adult speech (72.1% against 53.9%).
Two interpretations follow.
Part of the apparent error reflects genuinely ambiguous audio rather than a failure of the model.
And the room for improvement is uneven.

Adult and key-child error rates look similar in isolation, but on adult speech the pipeline is closer to the level of disagreement between human coders, whereas key-child speech is where an automated system has most ground to make up.
Coders and the pipeline also go wrong in different ways.

Coders' disagreements were mostly about which word was said on key-child speech (substitutions made up 19.7 of 35.4 points) and split almost evenly between substitutions and deletions on adult speech (21.3 and 19.7 of 53.9 points, with 12.9 points of insertions; Section 3.1).
The pipeline's errors were different.
For key-child and adult speech alike, its largest error type was deletion: it mostly missed speech that was there (Section 3.3).
Its errors therefore mainly shrink counts rather than inflate them; a pipeline that added speech could reach the same error rate while biasing downstream measures in the opposite direction.
The shrinkage is not equal across speakers and languages, however (the slopes in Section 3.5 range from 0.53 to 0.77), so comparisons of absolute counts between speakers still need care.
Agreement on who was speaking was also low among the coders, and simplifying the decision to key child versus adult did not help.

Most of this disagreement concerned whether someone was speaking at a given moment, not who: the measure compares coders wherever either one marked speech, and in 30% of comparisons one coder had marked speech where the other had marked none.
Where both coders marked speech, they agreed well on whether the speaker was the key child or an adult (α = .86); only one clip showed substantial confusion between the two.

Agreement on language was low mainly because coders disagreed about whether a stretch of speech could be classified at all; when both coders judged an utterance to be English or Spanish, their agreement on which language it was was high.
Yet agreement on how many words each speaker produced was very high.
Coders agreed closely on how much was said while disagreeing substantially on what was said and who said it.

Our WERs are much higher than the roughly 15% reported by Sun et al. (2024) for preschool classrooms and the 30% to 35% reported by Wu et al. (2025) for Mandarin-English telehealth sessions, and above the roughly 50% reported for caregiver-infant play (Tang et al., 2025), for daylong English recordings (Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025), and for all speech in naturalistic home recordings (Raviv et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Our WERs are much higher than the roughly 15% reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sun et al. (2024)</ref> for preschool classrooms and the 30% to 35% reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Wu et al. (2025)</ref> for Mandarin-English telehealth sessions, and above the roughly 50% reported for caregiver-infant play <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Tang et al., 2025)</ref>, for daylong English recordings <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kocharov & Räsänen, 2025)</ref>, and for all speech in naturalistic home recordings <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Raviv et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Those studies mostly evaluate adult speech in a single language, often recorded at closer range.

Our benchmark is harder in three ways: it scores child speech as well as adult speech, the audio is bilingual and code-switched, and the recorder is worn by the child in the home, so adults are often far from the microphone, with heavy background noise, overlapping talk, and short child utterances.

That the human coders also disagreed substantially on the same clips suggests the difficulty lies in the recordings rather than in the automated tools alone. Raviv et al. (2026) found the same in English home recordings, where two human transcribers differed from each other almost as much as WhisperX differed from them (WER 49% vs.

(2026)</ref> found the same in English home recordings, where two human transcribers differed from each other almost as much as WhisperX differed from them (WER 49% vs.

text.text: The present benchmark adds a measure of this difficulty for bilingual homes, with errors in transcription separated from errors in working out who is speaking.
Given the high WER, our second research question is central to whether the pipeline is useful.
Many research questions hinge on aggregate measures rather than individual words: the quantity of talk, its lexical diversity, and the proportion of each language a child hears and uses.

As Sun et al. (2024) and Kocharov and Räsänen (2025) argue, an automated transcript does not need to be right word for word to be useful; it needs to preserve the summary measures researchers plan to interpret.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sun et al. (2024)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kocharov and Räsänen (2025)</ref> argue, an automated transcript does not need to be right word for word to be useful; it needs to preserve the summary measures researchers plan to interpret.

text.text: On that test the pipeline partly succeeds.

Clip-level word counts correlated strongly with the manual counts, and summed over recordings VTC2 + WhisperX tracked the manual counts at least as closely as any other pipeline, including the one given the coders' boundaries (Section 3.5); with fourteen recordings, however, the ordering among pipelines should be interpreted with caution.

For studies that depend on how speakers compare with one another, such as relating input to outcomes or detecting change after an intervention, the pipeline largely preserves the information that matters.
The main limitation is in the absolute magnitude of counts rather than in ranking.
Because every slope fell below one, the pipeline preserves the relative ordering of clips but recovers a smaller share of the words as the amount of talk rises.

Type-based measures indexing lexical diversity performed better: their slopes were closer to one in every case, so the range of words a speaker used survives automation better than how much they spoke.
Importantly, both count-and type-based measures performed better than the two proportion-based measures we tested: the proportion of Spanish words and type-token ratio.
This is consistent with error compounding across the numerator and denominator of a proportion.
The type-token ratio, which Tang et al. (2025) report, agreed far less well and, in Spanish, was too high in the automated transcripts.
text.formatted: The type-token ratio, which <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Tang et al. (2025)</ref> report, agreed far less well and, in Spanish, was too high in the automated transcripts.

text.text: The ratio rises as a transcript gets shorter, and the pipeline returns only part of what was said, so it yields a smaller sample of talk that necessarily looks more varied per word.

Because clips vary substantially in how much speech they contain, this length sensitivity makes the ratio an unreliable summary here, which is why we treat the number of different words as the primary measure of lexical diversity.

De Houwer (2014) argued that percent exposure to each language is an inadequate measure of bilingual experience, because children with the same relative input can differ widely in their absolute input.

Her data from Belgian Dutch monolingual and Dutch-French bilingual families showed greater variability within groups than between groups and no significant differences in absolute maternal Dutch input, countering the common claim that bilinguals hear less input in each of their languages than monolinguals.
Other researchers have echoed this call and found that absolute measures were stronger predictors of child language skills than parent-reported relative exposure measures (Marchman et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Other researchers have echoed this call and found that absolute measures were stronger predictors of child language skills than parent-reported relative exposure measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Marchman et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In the current study, our selected pipeline recovered aggregate measures that index absolute input (word counts and lexical diversity in Spanish and English) better than measures of relative proportional exposure.
However, while correlations with human transcripts were high, our slopes suggest that for word counts, magnitudes at the higher end are compressed.

So while word-count measures produced by this pipeline can be used for within-group rankings, we do not recommend treating them as absolute quantities for individual children or for comparisons across samples without correcting for this error.

Because the relation between automated and manual counts was close to linear, a simple correction (dividing the automated count by the fitted slope after removing the intercept) could bring counts closer to their absolute values, provided the slope and intercept are estimated on expert-transcribed clips from the same population (Section 4.8).

In addition to absolute input, our approach also quantifies absolute child output in each language, which is particularly important in work on heritage language maintenance and on how children's active use of the heritage language shifts around school entry (Hammer et al., 2011).
text.formatted: In addition to absolute input, our approach also quantifies absolute child output in each language, which is particularly important in work on heritage language maintenance and on how children's active use of the heritage language shifts around school entry <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hammer et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: As with input, word counts of child output are best used for ranking clips rather than as exact quantities, especially for child Spanish, where the compression was greatest.

Lexical diversity, the most robust of our measures (Section 4.4), may capture dimensions of input and output quality in each language, and could provide a more fine-grained measure of bilingual experience at scale from naturalistic recordings.

The proportion of words in each language was the measure most affected by the pipeline's errors, as might be expected of a measure that depends on recognizing words, assigning speakers, and labeling languages all at once.
The pipeline understated the share of Spanish, and more for the key child than for adults.
The missing Spanish went to English: English errors were dominated by insertions, Spanish errors by deletions (Section 3.3).
The English error rate is sensitive to how little English there is: most clips contain only a handful of English words, so a few extra words produce a high error rate.
The underlying problem is not English transcription as such, but that the pipeline often produces English where the coders recorded none.
The failure analysis shows where this happens (Section 3.4).
It does not happen when languages are assigned to words, since the language labels almost always matched the language Whisper transcribed in.
The extra English is created during transcription.
Given a short, noisy, or wordless stretch of audio, Whisper falls back on a small set of English stock phrases, not on short English words in general.
Many of these phrases fall where the coders recorded no transcribable speech.

Some of this output may be television or other electronic speech, which the coders excluded and the speaker classifier does not always filter out (Section 2.1.2); the rest is talk the pipeline invents.
Where they do overlap real speech, that speech was mostly Spanish, so the pipeline replaces real talk, and a single error removes a Spanish word and adds an English one.
Stretches of detected speech for which no words were kept are not explained mainly by overlapping talk.
Faced with a short, noisy, or immature vocalization, Whisper either writes words in an unrelated language, which the pipeline discards, or writes a stock English phrase.
Either way, the speech that was there is lost: discarded stretches count as deletions, and stock phrases replace real words with English ones.

The key child's segments were the most likely to be left empty: more than one in three (1,432 of 3,816), against about one in four for other speakers (1,415 of 5,400), which may help explain why the Spanish shortfall is largest for the key child.
Stock phrases, by contrast, were not concentrated on the key child: 38% of them belonged to the key child, close to the key child's 41% share of all segments.
A difference in conventions adds to the shortfall: the coders treated language-neutral words inside Spanish talk as Spanish, whereas the pipeline counted them as English (Section 3.4).
All of these push in the same direction, which is why the pipeline underestimates how much Spanish a child hears and uses.

Systems designed for speakers who switch languages have tackled this same problem in other language pairs, through acoustic models that share sounds across both languages (Penagarikano et al., 2022 (Penagarikano et al., , 2024)), rewriting one language's words in the other's script during training (Yan et al., 2023), and automatic checking and correction of monolingual output (Hai et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Systems designed for speakers who switch languages have tackled this same problem in other language pairs, through acoustic models that share sounds across both languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Penagarikano et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Penagarikano et al., , 2024))</ref>, rewriting one language's words in the other's script during training <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Yan et al., 2023)</ref>, and automatic checking and correction of monolingual output <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hai et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our benchmark shows where such methods would help most for Spanish-English home audio: not in overall error, which discarding output in other languages barely changed, but in the word-by-word language decision on which every per-language measure depends.
Even with these biases, the pipeline provides something that existing automated tools cannot.
Systems that process daylong recordings return counts rather than transcripts, and do not identify which language is being spoken.

The LENA system, for example, reports adult word count, child vocalization count, and conversational turn count (Gilkerson et al., 2017), measures that have supported a large body of developmental research.
text.formatted: The LENA system, for example, reports adult word count, child vocalization count, and conversational turn count <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gilkerson et al., 2017)</ref>, measures that have supported a large body of developmental research.

text.text: For studies with monolingual populations, counts of this kind are often enough.
For a bilingual household, where the question is how much of each language a child hears and produces, they are not.
Our pipeline returns a time-stamped transcript with a language label on each utterance, so a researcher can count English and Spanish words, though within-utterance switches are not yet resolved.
Because every component is open, researchers can also inspect where errors occur and adapt the pipeline for a new population (Baker et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Because every component is open, researchers can also inspect where errors occur and adapt the pipeline for a new population <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baker et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The error rate is too high for the pipeline to replace human transcription.
Even so, it does recover language-specific measures that count-only systems cannot produce, with a bias that can be measured against a manual reference.
Our findings should be interpreted with several limitations in mind, each of which points toward future work that would address it.
First, the benchmark is 14 recordings from one Spanish-English community sample collected at baseline of a randomized controlled trial.

The size of the biases should be expected to change with dialect, recorder placement, age, and how often speakers switch languages, and will need re-estimating before the counts are used as corrected measures elsewhere.

Enlarging the benchmark beyond one community sample, and testing whether the measurement validity reported here holds across sites, is the most direct way to establish the generalizability of these estimates.
Second, we grouped individual speakers into the four categories VTC2 uses and, because the coders did not transcribe all other-child speech, left that category out of the speaker comparisons.
Measures that depend on input from siblings or other children are therefore not evaluated here.
It is also the category the reference supports least well, with the lowest agreement between coders of any speaker type (Section 3.1).

Evaluating sibling and peer input, and extending the measurement-validity analysis to utterance-level measures such as mean length of utterance, turn-taking, and response latency (Sun et al., 2024), would broaden the set of developmentally meaningful metrics the pipeline can reliably recover.
text.formatted: Evaluating sibling and peer input, and extending the measurement-validity analysis to utterance-level measures such as mean length of utterance, turn-taking, and response latency <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Sun et al., 2024)</ref>, would broaden the set of developmentally meaningful metrics the pipeline can reliably recover.

text.text: Third, language labels came from an off-the-shelf language detector applied to each automated utterance, so an utterance that switches language partway through is counted as one language.
The code-switching methods described in Section 4.6 could address this.
A component that decides the language of each word in Spanish-English speech, tested on this same benchmark, is a natural next step.
Fourth, the post-hoc pipelines labeled whole chunks of up to 30 seconds.

Assigning speakers word by word, using the timestamps WhisperX gives each word, might reduce the speaker errors described above; we tested the arrangement as it is commonly used, not every possible version of it.

A hybrid arrangement may combine the strengths of both: grouping consecutive VTC2 segments into windows of up to 30 seconds would give Whisper the longer context available in the post-hoc pipelines, while word timestamps would let each word keep the speaker label VTC2 assigned to it.
Fifth, word error rate is an imperfect summary for short, sparse child speech, where a handful of insertions can push the rate above 100%.
We report it because it is the field standard, and pair it with the word-count analysis for exactly this reason.
Sixth, the expert reference is itself imperfect, in ways that agreement on word counts alone does not reveal.
Coders agreed closely on how many words each speaker produced, but much less on who was speaking and on whether a stretch could be understood at all.
Because words marked unintelligible are removed from the reference before scoring (Section 2.4.1), disagreement about intelligibility changes which words a pipeline is scored against.
Our error rates are therefore measured against one plausible expert transcript, not against a single correct answer.
Seventh, two exclusions limit the estimates.
Eleven clips contained no transcribable words from the key child or adults and were dropped from the error rates, which may spare the weaker pipelines the spurious output they produced there.

And clips with no manual words in a language were left out of the word-count fits, so the slopes describe how well the pipeline recovers words that were spoken, not its tendency to report words that were never spoken.

Finally, the two post-hoc pipelines share one WhisperX transcript, so they separate the effect of the classifier from the effect of the order of the two steps but say nothing about the speech detector WhisperX uses (from pyannote.audio), which we did not vary.

We also left that detector active when WhisperX was given segments from the coders or from a voice type classifier, rather than passing those segments directly to Whisper; in VTC2 + WhisperX this affected at most 23 of the 2,847 segments for which no words were kept.
The results describe the current generation of open models (Whisper large-v3, VTC1, VTC2) and will need updating as these improve.
Off-the-shelf Whisper struggles with short, disfluent, high-pitch child speech (McGonigle et al., 2024), and further training
text.formatted: Off-the-shelf Whisper struggles with short, disfluent, high-pitch child speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(McGonigle et al., 2024)</ref>, and further training

text.text: WhisperX and the speaker classifier on Spanish-English child-centered recordings, kept separate from this benchmark so that it can still be used to test them, would target the transcription errors that remain even when the speech is found and labeled by the coders.
Two further directions follow from the findings.

Because every slope fell below one while correlations stayed high, the share of words the pipeline missed appears to grow with the amount of talk in a clip, which suggests that a correction estimated from a small set of clips transcribed by experts could recover approximately unbiased counts.
Testing whether such a correction carries over to other recorders, ages, and dialects would let the pipeline report amounts as well as rankings.

More reliable transcripts would also allow analyses beyond word counts: Liu and MacWhinney (2024) showed that Whisper, combined with Batchalign2 and Universal Dependencies parsing, can support morphosyntactic analysis of CHILDES data across 27 languages, which would connect daylong bilingual recordings to the CHILDES tools many developmental researchers already use.

For clinical applications such as bilingual assessment of suspected developmental language disorder (Albudoor & Peña, 2022; Baker et al., 2023), the pipeline is not yet suitable for decisions about individual children; it can support research comparisons where rank order suffices, while claims about the amount of each language wait for the steps above and for validation in a clinical sample.
text.formatted: For clinical applications such as bilingual assessment of suspected developmental language disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Albudoor & Peña, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baker et al., 2023)</ref>, the pipeline is not yet suitable for decisions about individual children; it can support research comparisons where rank order suffices, while claims about the amount of each language wait for the steps above and for validation in a clinical sample.

text.text: An open, inspectable pipeline makes that staged adoption possible, because its errors can be seen, measured, and improved rather than hidden inside a proprietary count.
Children's heritage language input and use often shift when they enter school, and studying this transition requires measuring how much of each language children hear and produce as it changes.
That measurement has not been possible at scale.

We benchmarked open, Whisper-based pipelines on 168 five-minute clips from 14 daylong Spanish-English home recordings, to our knowledge the first such benchmark for this language pair in naturalistic home audio, and found that automatic transcription can supply language-specific measures of input and output, albeit imperfectly.

Word error rate remains well above what two trained coders achieve on the same audio, and the errors are asymmetric: the pipeline misses Spanish words and adds English ones, so the heritage language is where the measures are least precise.
Yet counts of total words and of distinct words in each language track the manual counts closely enough to rank participants, with the number of distinct words recovered most reliably.
Whether speakers were identified before or after transcription mattered more for crediting words to the right speaker than which classifier was used.

For research on bilingual language environments, this approach offers a usable measure where none existed, with a bias that is systematic, measurable against a manual reference, and open to correction because every step can be inspected.

Ethics statement.

All procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston (HSC-MS-20-1134) and additional transcription and analyses were approved by the IRB of the University of Nevada, Las Vegas (UNLV-2025-172).

Written informed consent was obtained from the primary caregiver for each child's participation in the larger study, and separate written informed consent was obtained for participation in the daylong recording sub-study.
Consent was conducted in the caregiver's preferred language, most often Spanish, with written materials available in both Spanish and English.
All code and the derived datasets needed to reproduce our results are available at https://github.com/Surrain-Lab/bilingual-preschool-asr-benchmark.
text.formatted: All code and the derived datasets needed to reproduce our results are available at <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/Surrain-Lab/bilingual-preschool-asr-benchmark">https://github.com/Surrain-Lab/bilingual-preschool-asr-benchmark</ref>.

text.text: The underlying audio recordings and transcripts cannot be shared publicly because caregivers only consented to public release of de-identified data.

Daylong home recordings capture identifiable voices, names, and personal details from everyone in the household, including individuals who did not consent, and these cannot be removed without destroying the properties the recordings were collected to measure.
Caregivers consented to future research use, and we welcome inquiries from researchers interested in accessing the corpus.
Access requires a data use agreement and approval from the relevant institutional review boards.
Requests may be directed to the corresponding author.

90 %), principalement parce que WhisperX produisait de courtes phrases anglaises sur des segments audio brefs et peu clairs.

Des pipelines ouverts et inspectables peuvent mesurer, par langue, l'apport langagier des adultes et la production des enfants bilingues, mais les décomptes précis et les proportions linguistiques nécessitent une correction avant interprétation directe.
Ces estimations, issues d'une seule communauté espagnol-anglais, devront être réestimées dans d'autres populations.

ल�क्षत बच्चा: क्रमशः ७०% और ९०%)। इसका मु ख्य कारण यह था �क WhisperX ने छोटे और अस्पष्ट ऑ�डयो अं शों पर अं ग्रे ज़ी के छोटे वाक्यांश उत्पन्न �कए। खु ली और �नरीक्षण योग्य पाइपलाइनें �द्वभाषी पिरवे श में बच्चों को वयस्कों से �मलने वाले भा�षक इनपु ट और बच्चों द्वारा स्वयं बोली जाने वाली भाषा के भाषा-�व�शष्ट माप प्रदान कर सकती हैं । ले �कन शब्दों की सटीक सं ख्या और भाषाओं के अनु पात की सीधे व्याख्या करने से पहले उनमें सु धार आवश्यक है । एक ही स्पै �नश--अं ग्रे ज़ीभाषी समु दाय से प्राप्त इन अनु मानों का अन्य जनसमू हों में पु नः आकलन करना आवश्यक होगा। 1 Introduction setting.

text.text: Even the adult side of these interactions is difficult: in free play with infants aged 4 to 12 months, Whisper transcribed mothers' speech with a mean WER of 50%, with recurring problems in utterance segmentation, short utterances, the voice type classifiers and WhisperX expect.
